item.aggregated_output:
<<2:266 update 1, part 0 of 0..4>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
2:266/q01 What does the opening question convey? [أَيَوَدُّ أَحَدُكُمْ · rhetoric]
  2:266/q01/p1 It repudiates the prospect: no one would wish such a loss. — reasons: Al-Razi says the wish to avoid calamity is especially intense; Abu Hayyan says ahadukum distributes the question to each person; Bursavi distinguishes denying a wished prospect from denying an existing act, with two Arabic examples; Ibn Ashur compares the repudiating question at 49:12. Al-Biqai stresses the initially attractive orchard.
2:266/q02 What does the verb ayawaddu mean here? [أَيَوَدُّ · meaning]
  2:266/q02/p1 It means would love or wish. — reasons: Al-Razi defines wudd as complete love; al-Tabatabai adds an element of wishing.
2:266/q03 How is the opening verb read? [أَيَوَدُّ · readings] (turns on: Which verb expresses the wish.)
  2:266/q03/p1 The transmitted wording is ayawaddu, would wish. — reasons: Al-Alusi contrasts a report of Umar's alternate wording.
  2:266/q03/p2 Umar is reported to have read yuhibbu, would love. — reasons: Al-Alusi reports the reading.
2:266/q04 What is the janna in the scene? [جَنَّةٌ · meaning] (turns on: Whether janna itself names the vegetation or the land containing it.)
  2:266/q04/p1 A densely planted orchard or its covering trees. — reasons: Al-Tabrisi and al-Tabatabai explain that dense growth shades and covers the earth; al-Mawardi calls it an orchard. Bursavi and al-Alusi say taking it as trees lets rivers run beneath them directly; al-Alusi prefers this. Al-Tabatabai compares 23:50 and other gardens with water below.
  2:266/q04/p2 The land containing the trees. — reasons: Bursavi and al-Alusi say an omitted reference to trees is then needed to explain rivers beneath it; al-Alusi finds the tree sense more fitting.
2:266/q05 What variant is reported for janna? [جَنَّةٌ · readings] (turns on: Singular or plural noun.)
  2:266/q05/p1 A singular garden. — reasons: The verse wording contrasted with al-Hasan's plural reading.
  2:266/q05/p2 Al-Hasan reads jannat, gardens, in the plural. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan transmit it; al-Kashshaf also notes a gardens reading.
2:266/q06 What do nakhil and anab denote and how are they formed? [نَّخِيلٍ أَعْنَابٍ · meaning]
  2:266/q06/p1 Nakhil denotes date palms, as a collective noun or plural; anab denotes grapes, and anab is plural of inaba. — reasons: Abu Hayyan and al-Samin give both analyses of nakhil and record inba as the singular of grapes, with inba as a further extended form; al-Alusi reports the same morphology. Al-Tabrisi says nakhla is a palm and can be masculine or feminine, citing 69:7 and 54:20; al-Raghib derives nakhil from selected or sifted trees and notes its pollination and uses.
2:266/q07 Why are palms and vines named before the other fruits? [نَّخِيلٍ أَعْنَابٍ كُلِّ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ · rhetoric]
  2:266/q07/p1 They are the finest, most useful or prized core trees; the garden also contains other fruit. — reasons: Al-Mawardi notes flowing water as the orchard's best feature; al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Bursavi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi cite the trees' excellence. Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi say the whole palm is useful whereas the vine's chief benefit is its grapes, explaining the switch from tree to fruit. Al-Biqai says naming them specifies an earlier generic garden, 2:265; al-Harali likens the useful palm to a believer and the spreading vine to a pious believer.
2:266/q08 What does min in min nakhil do? [مِّن نَّخِيلٍۢ وَأَعْنَابٍۢ · grammar]
  2:266/q08/p1 It explains the orchard's predominant type or contents without excluding other plants. — reasons: Al-Tabrisi calls min explanatory. Al-Tabatabai cites the subsequent all fruits as proof that palms and vines are not exhaustive. Al-Samin parses min nakhil as a nominative adjective of janna.
2:266/q09 What does the phrase about rivers beneath the garden describe? [تَجْرِى مِن تَحْتِهَا ٱلْأَنْهَٰرُ · grammar] (turns on: The antecedent of the pronoun and the syntactic role of the river clause.)
  2:266/q09/p1 It describes the garden, with beneath referring to its trees. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya explicitly identifies the trees. Al-Samin permits a nominative adjectival clause or an accusative circumstantial clause from the described garden. Al-Tabrisi permits the garden as antecedent; al-Tabatabai explains water runs beneath dense tree growth. Al-Tabrisi defines anhar as broad channels of flowing water and adds a lexical aside that tahut means people low under others' feet and unnoticed.
  2:266/q09/p2 It may describe the date palms, with the pronoun returning to them. — reasons: Al-Tabrisi supplies this alternative antecedent.
  2:266/q09/p3 It may be the predicate of takuna. — reasons: Al-Samin reports this parse from Makki.
2:266/q10 What do the running rivers add to the image? [تَجْرِى مِن تَحْتِهَا ٱلْأَنْهَٰرُ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the detail is treated as orchard abundance or as a Paradise echo.)
  2:266/q10/p1 They make the orchard fertile, valuable and secure, making its loss more devastating. — reasons: Al-Mawardi calls water the best orchard feature; al-Razi says rivers and diverse produce complete its beauty and utility. Al-Biqai contrasts this irrigated orchard with the rain-fed ridge of 2:265, noting that irrigation failure is costlier.
  2:266/q10/p2 Running rivers also recall the recurring Paradise image. — reasons: Study Quran cites 2:25; al-Tabatabai compares 23:50 and gardens with water below.
2:266/q11 What does every fruit mean here? [مِن كُلِّ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ · meaning] (turns on: Whether thamarat names produce or the garden's benefits, and whether all is exhaustive.)
  2:266/q11/p1 Many different kinds of actual fruit, adding to palms and grapes. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi, al-Biqai and al-Baydawi take the clause as adding other varieties. Bursavi compares the broad expression in 47:15; al-Samin and al-Akhfash say exhaustive ownership is impossible. Al-Alusi rejects taking it literally as every individual fruit and rejects treating it merely as a generalizing restatement after the two named kinds.
  2:266/q11/p2 Fruits may stand for all the orchard's benefits. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf compares the two gardens in al-Kahf, 18:32 and 18:34; al-Alusi records this interpretation while favoring many actual varieties.
2:266/q12 How is min kull al-thamarat construed? [لَهُۥ فِيهَا مِن كُلِّ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ · grammar] (turns on: Whether min is licensed as an extra particle and whether all implies literal totality.)
  2:266/q12/p1 An omitted noun such as provision, fruit or food is understood before the prepositional phrase. — reasons: Abu Hayyan rejects extra min under Kufan and standard Basran conditions and supplies rizq or thamarat; al-Samin supplies rizq or fakiha, citing al-Nabigha and 37:164; Bursavi compares 37:164. Al-Alusi also gives this parse, with lahu as fronted predicate. Al-Samin notes that a prepositional phrase cannot literally be the subject.
  2:266/q12/p2 Min is extra, leaving the sense he has all kinds of fruit. — reasons: Al-Akhfash imposes no condition on extra min; al-Samin says all means abundance, since literal totality is impossible. Abu al-Baqa objects under both Sibawayh's and al-Akhfash's analyses if literal totality is implied, but permits it on the abundance sense. Abu Hayyan objects that neither Kufan nor normal Basran conditions are met.
2:266/q13 How does the past wording for old age fit the wish construction? [وَأَصَابَهُ ٱلْكِبَرُ · grammar] (turns on: Whether waw is circumstantial, or the past clause follows an implied law or the sense of the wish.)
  2:266/q13/p1 The waw introduces a circumstantial clause, with qad understood, describing the owner when he has the garden. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi give or permit this analysis. Al-Samin attaches it to ahadukum under yawaddu and compares 2:28 and 3:168; Abu Hayyan calls it the apparent reading.
  2:266/q13/p2 The past form has future force because wishes take an or law, whose constructions can interchange. — reasons: Al-Farra licenses the implied law after wudd and cites 30:51, 4:102, 68:9 and parallel mixing of forms at 52:40; Abu's reading of 4:102 has subjunctive fa-yamilu matching an, while indicative fa-yamiluna follows law. Al-Thalabi cites 3:30 and a poetry line; al-Wahidi cites 2:221, 30:51 and 68:9; al-Samin compares 11:98. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi adopt the same account. Al-Alusi reports Abu Hayyan's objection that it would make old age wished, which he finds unconvincing.
  2:266/q13/p3 The clause is coordinated by the sense: would one wish to have a garden and then have old age strike him? — reasons: Al-Kashshaf supplies the implicit hypothetical; al-Samin describes conversion from present sense to past. Abu al-Baqa calls this unnecessarily weak, while Abu Hayyan and al-Shaykh object that no one wishes old age itself. Al-Samin replies that the rejected wish is the combined state, not old age alone.
2:266/q14 Why say old age struck him, and what does old age imply? [وَأَصَابَهُ ٱلْكِبَرُ · rhetoric]
  2:266/q14/p1 It stresses the owner's reduced earning power and increased need, making the loss irreparable; asabahu makes the impact vivid. — reasons: Al-Mawardi adds that old age can erase memory of youthful labor, weaken hope and increase regret. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Bursavi, al-Tabatabai and Ibn Ashur stress inability to earn and the dependents' needs; al-Tabatabai contrasts young owners and elders with other support. Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi note the force of repeated asaba; Abu Hayyan compares the neighboring garden and stone examples, 2:264-265. Ibn Ashur cites al-Asha's poem for anticipation of harvest; al-Biqai emphasizes their lost wealth.
2:266/q15 What does al-kibar mean? [ٱلْكِبَرُ · meaning]
  2:266/q15/p1 Old age, a kind of greatness in age rather than multitude. — reasons: Abu Hay
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<2:266 update 1, part 1 of 0..4>>
yan glosses it as old age. Al-Tabrisi distinguishes kabir, size or age even of one house, from kathir, which necessarily implies number.
2:266/q16 Who are the weak offspring, and why mention them? [وَلَهُۥ ذُرِّيَّةٌۭ ضُعَفَآءُ · interpretation]
  2:266/q16/p1 Young, helpless dependents cannot work, support him or restore the orchard, intensifying his care and the loss. — reasons: Ibn Abbas calls them part of the parable. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi note a parent's special tenderness; al-Nasafi calls the garden their livelihood too. Al-Tabatabai says an elder with strong children could rely on them, unlike this owner. Ibn Ashur says daif can mean young, limited or poor, citing 2:282 and Abu Khalid al-Attabi's verse; Abu Hayyan also allows needy dependents. Bursavi and al-Alusi stress inability to earn.
2:266/q17 What forms are reported for the plural weak? [ضُعَفَآءُ · readings] (turns on: Equivalent plural forms and their readings.)
  2:266/q17/p1 Duafa is the verse form, a regular plural of daif. — reasons: Al-Akhfash compares fail plurals such as zurafa and zuraf. Al-Tabari compares 4:9; Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi recognize both plural patterns.
  2:266/q17/p2 Di'af or du'af is another regular plural form or variant reading. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf notes a weak offspring reading; al-Tabari cites 4:9 for diafa, while al-Akhfash, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi give the alternate plural patterns.
2:266/q18 How is the clause about offspring attached? [وَلَهُۥ ذُرِّيَّةٌۭ ضُعَفَآءُ · grammar]
  2:266/q18/p1 It is circumstantial, describing the owner when old age strikes. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi take the waw as circumstantial; al-Samin derives the circumstance from the pronoun in asabahu.
2:266/q19 What is an i'sar? [إِعْصَارٌۭ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the word itself is a general rotating wind, a hot samum, or a cold blast.)
  2:266/q19/p1 A fierce, rotating wind or whirlwind rising like a column, often lifting dust. — reasons: Al-Tabari gives its plural a'asir and cites Yazid ibn Mufarrigh; al-Zajjaj calls it zawba'a and cites an unnamed poet. Al-Thalabi cites al-Kumayt and Yazid ibn al-Muqri; Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Tabrisi, al-Samin and Ibn Abbas in al-Durr cite poetry or the wind proverb. Al-Jawhari adds umm zawba'a and says the name also belongs to a jinn chief. Al-Alusi describes colliding air currents, possible upward or downward motion and force enough to uproot trees or snatch boats. Al-Tabatabai describes a twisting dust column between earth and sky.
  2:266/q19/p2 It is specifically the deadly hot wind called samum. — reasons: Al-Suddi gives this gloss through al-Mawardi; Ibn Atiyya calls the whirlwind violent and scorching. Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi in al-Qurtubi describe the hot wind. Ibn Ashur identifies a violent hot wind likened to fire or samum.
  2:266/q19/p3 It is a cold blast or frost. — reasons: Al-Hasan gives this second gloss in Ibn Abi Hatim; al-Hasan and al-Dahhak elsewhere describe cold within the whirlwind.
2:266/q20 Why is the whirlwind called i'sar? [إِعْصَارٌۭ · meaning] (turns on: Which observed squeezing or twisting motivates the word; Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi disagree about the cloth derivation.)
  2:266/q20/p1 Its coiling motion resembles cloth being wrung. — reasons: Al-Mawardi cites a poem; al-Mahdawi gives the derivation in Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi. Ibn Atiyya calls it weak, while al-Qurtubi endorses it as observable; al-Samin, al-Alusi and al-Tabatabai also mention twisting cloth.
  2:266/q20/p2 The wind squeezes or compresses clouds or bodies. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya cites the wind proverb and relates mu'sirat either to pregnant rain clouds or clouds compressed by winds; he reports al-Anbari and Ibn Sida's alternatives, the latter taking mu'sirat as winds. Al-Qurtubi repeats the derivations. Abu Hayyan describes a hot cloud-compressing wind; al-Harali links the name to squeezing hidden contents.
2:266/q21 What is the fire in the whirlwind? [فِيهِ نَارٌۭ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the destructive fire is heat, cold, actual flame, lightning, or Hell's breath.)
  2:266/q21/p1 Scorching samum or exceptionally hot wind. — reasons: Ibn Abbas repeatedly calls it samum; Qatada calls the wind a carrier of it and al-Suddi distinguishes wind from its fire. Al-Tabari also transmits Ibn Abbas that jinn-creating samum is one seventieth of fire; Ibn Atiyya attributes this proportion to Ibn Masud and identifies the Fire as the afterlife's, while Abu Hayyan repeats it. Ibn Ashur says the wind is emphatically likened to fire. Al-Alusi says the indefinite fire magnifies it.
  2:266/q21/p2 Biting cold, frost or hail that burns and ruins the garden. — reasons: Al-Hasan gives bitter cold in Abd al-Razzaq and severe cold and hail in al-Tabari; al-Dahhak agrees. Al-Harali calls a cold edge a kind of fire.
  2:266/q21/p3 It may be literal fire carried by the wind. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya allows literal fire, and al-Tabrisi states that the wind's fire burns the garden.
  2:266/q21/p4 It may be lightning. — reasons: Abu Hayyan records this alternate explanation.
  2:266/q21/p5 Its heat or cold may be a breath of Hell. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya cites a Prophetic report about intense heat and the Fire's complaint; al-Qurtubi reports his view and the prayer-delaying report.
2:266/q22 How is fihi nar parsed? [فِيهِ نَارٌۭ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the locative itself modifies the whirlwind or belongs to a modifying clause.)
  2:266/q22/p1 Fihi is a modifying locative phrase and nar is its raised subject. — reasons: Al-Nasafi says the locative functions as an adjective of i'sar. Abu Hayyan says the masculine pronoun agrees with masculine i'sar. Al-Samin prefers this direct adjectival parse for simplicity.
  2:266/q22/p2 Fihi is the predicate of nar, and the entire clause modifies i'sar. — reasons: Abu Hayyan and al-Samin allow this analysis; al-Samin prefers the simpler direct locative adjective.
2:266/q23 What do the successive fa and burning verb convey? [فَأَصَابَهَآ فَٱحْتَرَقَتْ · grammar]
  2:266/q23/p1 The storm strikes after the garden has become useful, then the garden burns up as the intransitive result of burning it. — reasons: Abu Hayyan reads the successive fa as sequence after ripening; he and al-Samin distinguish intransitive ihtaraqa from transitive ahraqa. Al-Samin gives the burning then burned-up sequence; both cite the expression harqa nab and a poetic line with nominative or accusative nab. Ibn Abi Hatim reports Ibn Abbas's direct gloss that the garden itself burned. Ibn Kathir says fruit and trees were consumed. Abu al-Baqa instead coordinates the storm clause with the earlier adjectival garden description.
2:266/q24 What does thus refer back to and what are the signs explained? [كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمُ ٱلْءَايَٰتِ · referent] (turns on: How broad the backward reference is.)
  2:266/q24/p1 The preceding parables and disclosures, including spending, Abraham and the ruined town, clarify religious proofs. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj includes charity and struggle and says these establish oneness, messengership, reward and punishment. Al-Wahidi cites 2:258-259 for oneness; al-Tabrisi includes all preceding disclosures. Ibn Atiyya says thus points to the parables just described. Bursavi includes striving, spending, Abraham and Ezra. Al-Nasafi speaks of monotheism and religion. Ibn Ashur says concrete images bring abstract truths near, citing 2:143; Abu Hayyan lists allusion, simile, ellipsis, specification, parable and metaphor.
  2:266/q24/p2 It points specifically to what has just been mentioned. — reasons: Sa'id ibn Jubayr gives this gloss; al-Samin says the closing phrase was discussed earlier.
2:266/q25 What reflection does the closing appeal seek? [لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَفَكَّرُونَ · interpretation] (turns on: Which lesson of the parable the reflective command highlights.)
  2:266/q25/p1 Understand the parables, take warning or guidance, and act or obey accordingly. — reasons: Mujahid glosses reflection as obedience; Qatada cites 29:43 that the learned understand parables. Al-Mawardi gives taking a lesson or finding guidance, while Ibn Kathir and al-Durr urge application. Al-Biqai and al-Harali say worship needs thought about beginnings and outcomes; a sage reverses the sequence of thought and work. Elmalili defines thought as arranging known matters to discover unknown ones and says to draw analogies and act. Ibn Atiyya explains perhaps as human hope that reflection prepares a person for thought.
  2:266/q25/p2 Think about the world's passing and the afterlife's permanence, then turn toward the latter. — reasons: Ibn Abbas contrasts the two realms; Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi draw the practical consequence of seeking what lasts rather than grieving over worldly loss.
  2:266/q25/p3 Turn back to God's majesty and lordship rather than taking other protectors. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi gives this further application.
2:266/q26 What does perhaps imply about God's intention? [لَعَلَّكُمْ · theology] (turns on: How a particle of hope is understood when spoken by God.)
  2:266/q26/p1 It expresses hope from the human perspective, since reflection may make one fit to understand. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya explains the phrasing this way.
  2:266/q26/p2 It implies that God intends all people to believe. — reasons: Al-Razi reports this Mu'tazilite argument from the apparent hope particle and notes that hope is inappropriate to God.
2:266/q27 What does the ruined garden represent? [* · interpretation] (turns on: The context of spending, the scope of the image, and whether ruin comes from insincere giving, harm, later sin, neglected obedience or unbelief.)
  2:266/q27/p1 Showy or insincere charity, whose apparent reward vanishes at Judgment when needed most. — reasons: Al-Suddi repeatedly identifies another parable for ostentatious spending. Al-Tabari calls him closest to correct; Ibn Atiyya reports but resists making it a second separate showmanship im

<<2:266 update 1, part 2 of 0..4>>
age. Al-Tabari describes worldly praise and protection as the garden's apparent fruit; al-Kashshaf and al-Razi widen this to deeds done without God's pleasure. Al-Razi cites 39:47 and 25:23. The old owner's helplessness images inability to repent or recover reward after death.
  2:266/q27/p2 Charity spoiled by reminders, insults or injury to its recipient. — reasons: Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari ground this in 2:264; al-Tabari prefers the contextual connection, while Ibn Atiyya prefers Ibn Zayd over a separate showmanship parable. Al-Tabatabai says a spoiled deed cannot be made sound again. Ibn Ashur says this is the unstated counterpart to sincere giving; al-Biqai says abuse ruins the giver's hope.
  2:266/q27/p3 Good works begun sincerely but wiped out by later sin or a corrupt final act. — reasons: The Umar-Ibn Abbas exchange describes a wealthy worshipper drawn by Satan into sins; other tellings specify evil near death, shirk or a major sin, dying an unbeliever, or final wrongdoing represented by the fiery storm. Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi favor this scope; al-Alusi appeals to Ibn Abbas's standing and Umar's approval. Al-Tabrisi says this and the other major readings all fit. The work is most needed at death or Judgment, when restoration is impossible.
  2:266/q27/p4 Neglect of obedience while absorbed in worldly life, discovered with regret after death. — reasons: Mujahid repeatedly gives this sense; Qatada and al-Rabi warn of dying in error and sin. Ibn Jurayj adds a youth and wealth wasted without action until both disappear. Al-Tabrisi says this and the other major readings fit the wording.
  2:266/q27/p5 The disbeliever or hypocrite who expects benefit from worldly works but arrives with no good and no second chance. — reasons: Muqatil likens the garden to a disbeliever's deeds, stressing that he cannot return to youth to replant or to life to amend. Ibn Abbas contrasts the believer's stored eternal honor with a wealthy disbeliever's lasting punishment for boasting and doubting God's meeting. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir also apply it to the unbeliever; Ibn Atiyya says the broad image covers any hypocrite or unbeliever with apparent works.
  2:266/q27/p6 More generally, it images any loss of needed deeds or blessing at the moment when recovery is impossible. — reasons: Ibn Abbas and Umar also speak simply of deeds; al-Hasan emphasizes maximum need at life's end. Ibn Atiyya says the wording can cover every applicable case, and al-Tabrisi accepts three named applications. Qatada cites 29:43 for understanding parables. Al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Biqai and Elmalili dwell on the anguish of lost livelihood and reward.
  2:266/q27/p7 It may also image a polity prepared for blessing but ruined by coercive injustice, unbelief, immorality and lost resolve. — reasons: Elmalili says this devastates worldly and afterlife prospects.
2:266/q28 How does this parable connect to its surrounding verses? [* · links] (turns on: How narrowly to tie the image to showmanship and how widely to read its place in the charity passage.)
  2:266/q28/p1 It continues the warning in 2:264 that reproach, harm or hypocrisy can nullify charity. — reasons: Al-Tabari links the bare stone to the burned garden and prefers the immediate charity context; Ibn Zayd, al-Thalabi, al-Baghawi, al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi, al-Biqai, Ibn Ashur and al-Tabatabai likewise trace the warning to 2:264. Ibn Ashur contrasts the ruined garden with fruitful sincere spending at 2:261 and 2:265; al-Harali contrasts ruin from below at the root in the first garden with harm from above at the branches in this one.
  2:266/q28/p2 It is another specific parable for ostentatious giving beside the earlier stone image. — reasons: Al-Suddi's formulation is preferred by al-Tabari. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report al-Tabari's preference but prefer the broader immediate-context connection; Ibn Atiyya disputes treating it as a second separate showmanship parable.
  2:266/q28/p3 It leads into instruction about the form and recipients of obligatory and voluntary spending. — reasons: Elmalili describes the transition toward where, how and to whom to give.
2:266/q29 What happened in the report of Umar asking about the parable? [* · reports] (turns on: The reports vary in Ibn Abbas's wording and whether Umar or Ibn Abbas states the late-life analogy.)
  2:266/q29/p1 Umar pressed the Companions for an answer, Ibn Abbas interpreted deeds ruined after obedience by Satan-led sins, and Umar approved. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi describe Umar's anger when they deferred instead of saying whether they knew; Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Kashshaf, Ibn Kathir, al-Biqai, al-Durr, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur transmit the wealthy worshipper explanation. Al-Qurtubi calls it an established Bukhari report, Ibn Kathir says al-Bukhari alone transmits this interpretation, al-Biqai specifies Bukhari's tafsir, and al-Alusi also names al-Hakim and Ibn Jarir. Al-Durr adds that Ibn Abbas first whispered his thought. Baghawi transmits a version through Ubayd ibn Umayr in which Ibn Abbas says show-off and Umar gives the wealthy worshipper analogy.
  2:266/q29/p2 Another telling has Ibn Abbas say a person ends a long good life with evil when deeds are most needed, and Umar accepts or marvels. — reasons: Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya transmit this formulation. Ibn Abi Mulayka attributes the late-life summary to Umar in Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi. Al-Durr gives several versions, including an evil final deed and persistent late sin; al-Alusi reports Ata's version.
2:266/q30 What other transmitted reports are brought to bear on this verse? [* · reports] (turns on: These are separate reports used as illustrations, not rival accounts of one event.)
  2:266/q30/p1 The Prophet prayed for his broadest provision in old age near life's end. — reasons: Ibn Kathir attributes the report to al-Hakim; al-Durr transmits it from Aisha.
  2:266/q30/p2 A Prophetic report associates intense heat with Hell's breath and the Fire's complaint. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya cites it to illuminate the wind's heat; al-Qurtubi adds delaying prayer in severe heat.
  2:266/q30/p3 Ikrima says every worldly kind of tree exists in Paradise, even colocynth. — reasons: Ibn Abi Hatim transmits the statement beside the garden's fruits.
  2:266/q30/p4 Ibn Abbas also describes a man who wastes his garden in youth and loses it in old age, when weak children cannot help restore or support him. — reasons: Ibn Kathir preserves this as an alternate Ibn Abbas report.
  2:266/q30/p5 Ali asked forgiveness for devotions whose intention his heart later contradicted. — reasons: Al-Qashani uses the prayer to illustrate later inner corruption of good action.
  2:266/q30/p6 The Prophet advised Muadh to make religion sincere so even little work suffices. — reasons: Bursavi cites the instruction given when Muadh was sent to Yemen.
2:266/q31 What inward process can destroy a deed or spiritual progress? [* · inward] (turns on: Whether the inner ruin is corruption of a deed's intention or reversal of a seeker's ascent.)
  2:266/q31/p1 Ego, self-regard or ostentation turns a good deed's inner motions into Satan's whirlwind, and its fire consumes the deed. — reasons: Al-Qashani includes charity done for God's pleasure before the ego reappears; he cites Ali's prayer about intentions later contradicted by the heart.
  2:266/q31/p2 A seeker rises toward the divine unseen realm, turns back to worldly illusion, and loses the effort. — reasons: Al-Baydawi likens the scattered effort to dust; Bursavi gives the same spiritual parallel.
2:266/q32 How should a giver protect work from the ruin pictured here? [* · interpretation]
  2:266/q32/p1 Keep sincerity at the root of worship and resist ostentation before and during action. — reasons: Bursavi quotes Qushayri's contrast of sincere and hypocritical spending, flourishing crops and ruined bargains. Bursavi says fruits depend on roots, names love of the world and immediate pleasure as chief causes, and counsels examining the heart before worship, removing showy thoughts and resisting them. He distinguishes expecting notice, desiring praise and status, then accepting that desire. Al-Tabatabai adds love of wealth and status, pride, conceit and miserliness, saying reflection exposes their harm.
2:266/q33 How is the wider spending passage organized? [* · links]
  2:266/q33/p1 It forms a connected teaching on the purpose, manner, quality, recipient and reward of giving. — reasons: Al-Tabatabai says the connected themes suggest revelation as one unit: seven-hundredfold or greater growth, sincere fruitfulness, loss through ostentation or harm, giving good wealth, aid to the needy detained in God's path, and great reward. He orders these as giving for God, without reproach or injury, from good property, to the needy, for reward.
